Main article: [2023 United Auto Workers strike](/wiki/2023_United_Auto_Workers_strike "2023 United Auto Workers strike")

The 2023 strike launched by the UAW was the first strike against all three major American automakers in history. Then-recently elected UAW president [Shawn Fain](/wiki/Shawn_Fain "Shawn Fain") stated that he was "fed up" with the current situation between workers and automakers; Fain specifically blasted the tiered workers system at automakers, failure for automakers to keep wages up with inflation, pensions, as well as the introduction of a [four-day workweek](/wiki/Four-day_workweek "Four-day workweek") as opposed to the five-day workweek. GM CEO [Mary Barra](/wiki/Mary_Barra "Mary Barra") protested that her company offered an "unprecedented deal" which gave workers 20% raises as well as "world-class" healthcare. Barra further stated that meeting all 1,000 plus demands would bankrupt the company and cost over $100 billion.[[256]](#cite_note-256)[[257]](#cite_note-257)

Mercury is one of four [terrestrial planets](/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet") in the [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"), which means it is a rocky body like Earth. [Tornadoes](/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") and [waterspouts](/wiki/Waterspout "Waterspout") may lift up animals into the air and deposit them miles away.

French physicist [André-Marie Ampère](/wiki/Andr%C3%A9-Marie_Amp%C3%A8re "André-Marie Ampère") (1775–1836) was among the first scientists to take accounts of raining animals. Addressing the Society of Natural Science, Ampère suggested that at times frogs and toads roam the countryside in large numbers, and that violent winds could pick them up and carry them great distances.[[3]](#cite_note-Ampère-3)

After a reported rain of fish in Singapore in 1861, French naturalist [Francis de Laporte de Castelnau](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Louis_de_la_Porte,_comte_de_Castelnau "François Louis de la Porte, comte de Castelnau") speculated that a migration of [walking catfish](/wiki/Walking_catfish "Walking catfish") had taken place, dragging themselves over land from one puddle to another, following the rain.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The likeliest explanation for many of the supposed cases is that there is no falling happening at all and the animals are driven along by winds or a deluge of some sort.[[9]](#cite_note-Nobel_2014-9) This explanation accounts for the prevalence of reports that just a single species or type of animal raining from the sky. In several occurrences within two weeks of October, 1987, people in three towns of [Gloucestershire](/wiki/Gloucestershire "Gloucestershire"), [England](/wiki/England "England") named [Stroud](/wiki/Stroud "Stroud"), [Cirencester](/wiki/Cirencester "Cirencester"), and [Cheltenham](/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham") reported heavy rain fall that also brought down dozens of tiny pink frogs.
